docs.title: Kelora Documentation
docs.text:
Scriptable log processor for the command line.

Kelora parses log streams into structured events and lets you filter, transform, and analyze them using embedded Rhai scripting with 40+ built-in functions.

Experimental Tool

Kelora is an experimental tool under active development. APIs may change without notice.

docs.title: What is Kelora?
docs.text:
Kelora turns log lines into structured events you can manipulate programmatically:

  • Parse - JSON, logfmt, syslog, CSV/TSV, Apache/Nginx combined format, or custom column specs
  • Filter - Keep only events that match your conditions
  • Transform - Enrich, redact, extract, or restructure event data
  • Analyze - Track metrics, compute aggregations, detect patterns
  • Output - Default key=value format, JSON, CSV, or custom templates

docs.title: Flexible Parsing
docs.text:
Built-in parsers for common formats:

  • JSON (-f json) - Standard JSON logs
  • Logfmt (-f logfmt) - key=value format
  • Syslog (-f syslog) - RFC3164 and RFC5424
  • Combined (-f combined) - Apache/Nginx access logs
  • CSV/TSV (-f csv, -f tsv) - Tabular data
  • Custom (-f cols:<spec>) - Define your own column-based format

docs.title: Powerful Scripting
docs.text:
Embedded Rhai scripting with 40+ built-in functions:

  • String manipulation: extract_re(), parse_json(), contains()
  • Type conversion: to_int(), to_float(), to_bool()
  • Time handling: parse_datetime(), format_datetime(), now_utc()
  • Metrics tracking: track_count(), track_sum(), track_avg()
  • Array processing: sorted(), unique(), emit_each()
  • Field operations: get_path(), has_path(), path_equals()

docs.title: Performance Options
docs.text:
• Sequential mode (default) - Maintains order, lower memory
  • Parallel mode (--parallel) - Higher throughput, uses multiple cores
  • Streaming - Process data as it arrives
  • Batch - Process large archives efficiently

docs.title: Resilient Processing
docs.text:
• Skip unparseable lines by default
  • Continue processing on script errors
  • Strict mode (--strict) for fail-fast behavior
  • Comprehensive error reporting

docs.title: Kelora Cookbook
docs.text: Quick, runnable patterns for common log-processing workflows. Every example stays close to the built-in sample logs in examples/ so you can try them without touching production data.

docs.title: Narrow to interesting events
docs.text:
kelora -j examples/simple_json.jsonl --filter 'e.service == "database"' \
  --exec 'e.duration_s = e.get_path("duration_ms", 0) / 1000' \
  --keys timestamp,message,duration_s

docs.title: Slice by text before parsing
docs.text:
cat examples/prefix_docker.log | \
  kelora --extract-prefix container --prefix-sep ' | ' \
    --filter 'e.container == "web_1"'

docs.title: Tail logs and count incidents
docs.text:
tail -f examples/simple_logfmt.log | \
  kelora -f logfmt \
    --filter '"duration" in e && e.duration.to_int_or(0) >= 1000' \
    --exec 'track_count("slow_requests")' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Sliding-window anomaly detection
docs.text:
kelora -f syslog examples/simple_syslog.log \
  --filter '"msg" in e && e.msg.contains("Failed login")' \
  --window 5 \
  --exec 'let hits = window_values("msg").filter(|m| m.contains("Failed login"));\
           if hits.len() >= 3 { e.alert = true; }' \
  --filter 'e.alert == true'

docs.title: Add derived attributes
docs.text:
kelora -f combined examples/web_access_large.log.gz \
  --exec 'let status = e.status.to_int();\
          e.family = if status >= 500 { "server_error" } else if status >= 400 { "client_error" } else { "ok" };'

docs.title: Anonymise while keeping linkability
docs.text:
kelora -j examples/security_audit.jsonl \
  --exec 'e.user_alias = pseudonym(e.user, "users"); e.ip_masked = e.ip.mask_ip(1)' \
  --keys timestamp,event,user_alias,ip_masked

docs.title: Flatten arrays safely
docs.text:
kelora -j examples/json_arrays.jsonl \
  --exec 'emit_each(e.get_path("users", []))' \
  --keys id,name,score

docs.title: Multi-level fan-out with context
docs.text:
kelora -j examples/fan_out_batches.jsonl \
  --exec 'let ctx = #{batch_id: e.batch_id}; emit_each(e.orders, ctx)' \
  --exec 'let ctx2 = #{batch_id: e.batch_id, order_id: e.order_id}; emit_each(e.items, ctx2)' \
  --keys batch_id,order_id,sku,qty,price

docs.title: Rolling average on numeric streams
docs.text:
kelora -j examples/window_metrics.jsonl \
  --window 5 \
  --exec 'let values = window_numbers("value");\
           if values.len() == 5 { let total = 0.0; for v in values { total += v; }\
                                  e.moving_avg = total / values.len(); }'

docs.title: Histogram buckets per request family
docs.text:
kelora -f combined examples/web_access_large.log.gz \
  --metrics \
  --exec 'track_bucket("status_family", (e.status / 100 * 100).to_int_or(0))' \
  --end 'for (bucket, counts) in metrics.status_family {\
           print(bucket.to_string() + ": " + counts.to_string()); }' \
  -F none

docs.title: Type annotations on CSV/TSV
docs.text:
kelora -f "csv status:int bytes:int duration_ms:int" examples/simple_csv.csv
kelora -f "tsv: user_id:int success:bool" examples/simple_tsv.tsv

docs.title: Column specs with joins and strict mode
docs.text:
kelora -f "cols:date(2) level *msg:string" examples/cols_fixed.log
kelora -f "csv status:int" --strict examples/errors_csv_ragged.csv

docs.title: 7. Performance Checklist
docs.text:
1. Streaming? stay sequential (default) and emit to stdout.
  2. Archives? add --parallel --stats, monitor stats for skew, then tune --batch-size/--batch-timeout.
  3. Windowed workloads? prefer smaller windows (--window 50) or sample events upstream to curb memory.
  4. Verbose scripts? switch to -q once pipelines stabilise to cut stderr noise.
  5. Need ordering guarantees? skip --unordered; otherwise enable it for faster parallel flushes.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting Cheats
docs.text:
• Diagnose parse hiccups with -F inspect or --verbose.
  • Timestamp woes? add --ts-field, --ts-format, or --input-tz (see kelora --help-time).
  • Rhai panics? wrap lookups with e.get_path("field", ()) and numeric conversions with to_int_or.
  • Gzip everywhere? nothing to add: Kelora auto-detects compressed input.

docs.title: Kelora Integration Guide
docs.text:
Composing with the right tools makes logs sing.

Kelora is the log scalpel — it shapes raw text into structured events. Once logs are clean, other tools can filter, analyze, or visualize them with elegance. This guide shows how Kelora pairs with a handful of timeless allies that share its spirit: small, sharp, and scriptable.

docs.title: 🧩 Core Idea
docs.text: Kelora normalizes. Others analyze. Use it to turn noise into structure — JSONL, TSV, or logfmt — then pipe the result onward. Every tool below does one thing brilliantly.

docs.title: jq / jaq — Deep JSON slicing
docs.text:
Kelora emits JSONL; jq dissects it.

kelora -f combined -F json --filter 'e.status >= 500' \
| jq -r '. | [.ts, .path, .status] | @tsv'
  • jq’s power meets Kelora’s discipline — no malformed JSON, ever.
  • jaq is a Rust rewrite that’s orders faster; perfect for big logs.

💡 Bonus: jq can stream-parse gigabytes; Kelora’s --parallel keeps up.

docs.title: qsv — Lightning CSV analytics
docs.text:
For top-Ns, counts, or quick histograms:

kelora -f json -F csv --keys ts,service,status \
| qsv frequency --column service --limit 10
  • qsv runs Rust-fast and memory-light.
  • Combine with --stats or --metrics for instant dashboards without dashboards.

💡 Tip: use kelora --exec 'e.day = e.ts.format("%F")' to enrich timestamps for time-based grouping.

docs.title: VisiData — Interactive spelunking
docs.text:
Turn structured output into an instant spreadsheet:

kelora -f logfmt -F tsv --keys ts,level,msg | vd -
  • Sort, pivot, graph — all inside your terminal.
  • Streams stay live: press g# for group counts, / for filtering, or Shift+G for plots.

💡 Pair with: --window in Kelora to feed contextual streams into VisiData for exploration.

docs.title: spyql — SQL on streams
docs.text:
SQL aggregation, no database needed:

kelora -j -F json --keys ts,user,action \
| spyql -O table "SELECT user, COUNT(*) c FROM input GROUP BY user ORDER BY c DESC"
  • Feels like SQLite, runs like awk.
  • Works perfectly with kelora --exec transformations.

💡 Mix-in: emit_each() fan-outs from arrays, turning nested JSON into rows for SpyQL to count.

docs.title: rare — Regex histograms
docs.text:
Quick regex-driven insights:

kelora -f syslog -k msg | rare -r 'error|warn|timeout'
  • Shows dominant patterns — perfect for first-look diagnostics.
  • Add --since/--until to narrow the temporal window.

💡 Pro tip: Pipe structured Kelora fields into rare -r for statistical debugging.

docs.title: 🏗️ Unix Classics — The Original Power Tools
docs.text: Kelora speaks fluent POSIX.

docs.title: awk — Stream arithmetic
docs.text:
kelora -F tsv --keys ts,service,status \
| awk -F'\t' '$3 >= 500 {print $1, $2, $3}'
  • For quick ratios, deltas, or counters — awk still rules.
  • Kelora’s clean TSV guarantees no quoting nightmares.

💡 Enrich first: --exec 'e.delta = e.end.to_int() - e.start.to_int()' then post-process in awk.

docs.title: cut / sort / uniq — The timeless trio
docs.text:
kelora -F tsv --keys service \
| cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
  • Minimal, composable, transparent.
  • Kelora’s field normalization makes these safe and predictable.

💡 Trick: kelora -F tsv --keys ip | sort | uniq -c gives quick top IPs from any format.

docs.title: sqlite3 — Instant structured DB
docs.text:
kelora -F tsv --keys ts,service,status > events.tsv
sqlite3 :memory: <<'SQL'
.mode tabs
.import events.tsv events
SELECT service, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY service ORDER BY 2 DESC;
SQL
  • Treat logs as tables; run ad-hoc joins or time filters.
  • SQLite loves Kelora’s TSV output — no schema headaches.

💡 Hack: combine with kelora --exec 'e.day = e.ts.format("%F")' for date-based rollups.

docs.title: lnav — The Living Log Viewer
docs.text:
kelora -f json -F json app.log | lnav -i json
  • lnav auto-detects timestamps, builds timelines, and runs SQL.
  • Kelora feeds it pristine structure — lnav handles the live browsing.

💡 Run inside lnav:

;SELECT level, COUNT(*) FROM log GROUP BY level;

docs.title: klogg — GUI grep for giants
docs.text:
kelora -f syslog --filter 'e.level == "error"' > errors.log
klogg errors.log
  • Opens terabyte logs instantly.
  • Use it when less starts to sweat.

💡 Combine with --pretty-ts for readable time context in visual searches.

docs.title: tailspin — Streaming color
docs.text:
kelora -f combined | tailspin
  • Colorized, leveled tails for real-time debugging.
  • Matches Kelora’s --realtime mode perfectly.

docs.title: Benthos — Stream orchestration
docs.text:
benthos -c benthos.yaml | kelora -f json --exec 'e.env = "prod"' -F json
  • Benthos handles I/O, Kelora handles semantics.
  • Together they form a declarative, testable log refinery.

docs.title: From chaos to clarity
docs.text:
tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log \
| kelora -f combined --filter 'e.status >= 500' \
  --keys ts,path,status -F csv \
| qsv frequency -c path --limit 20

Or interactively:

kelora -f json -F tsv --keys ts,level,msg app.log | vd -

Or classically:

kelora -f logfmt -F tsv --keys level | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c

Kelora parses and filters — everything else explores and aggregates.

docs.title: 🌐 Inbound & Outbound
docs.text:
Inbound: raw logs, JSONL, syslog, logfmt, csv/tsv, gzipped streams. → Preprocessors like jc (for shell command output) or evtx2json (for Windows event logs) slot right in.

Outbound: -F json, -F csv, or -F tsv depending on what follows. Use --keys, --filter, and --exec to shape before export.

docs.title: 🧘 Philosophy Recap
docs.text:
Kelora doesn’t compete — it completes. It’s the prelude to every great analysis: clean in, clean out. Logs, refined to truth. Then — pass them on.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Understanding Kelora's error handling modes and how to diagnose issues.

docs.title: Processing Modes
docs.text:
Kelora offers two error handling modes:

Mode Behavior Use Case Resilient (default) Skip errors, continue processing Production log analysis, exploratory work Strict (--strict) Fail-fast on errors Data validation, CI/CD pipelines

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In resilient mode (default), Kelora continues processing even when errors occur:

  • Parse errors: Skip unparseable lines, continue with next line
  • Filter errors: Treat as false, skip event
  • Transform errors: Return original event unchanged (atomic rollback)
  • Summary: Show error count at end

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Analyzing messy production logs
  • Exploratory data analysis
  • Real-time log streaming
  • Mixed format log files

docs.title: Example Behavior
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int() * 2'

Input: 

{"value": "123"}
{"value": "invalid"}
{"value": "456"}

Output: 

result=246
(skipped - error converting "invalid")
result=912

Summary: 

🔹 Processed 3 lines, 2 events output, 1 error

docs.title: Error Recording
docs.text:
Errors are recorded but don't stop processing:

> kelora -j app.log --filter 'e.timestamp.to_unix() > 1000000'

If e.timestamp is missing or invalid: - Filter evaluates to false - Event is skipped - Error is recorded - Processing continues

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In strict mode (--strict), Kelora fails immediately on the first error:

  • Parse errors: Show error, abort immediately
  • Filter errors: Show error, abort immediately
  • Transform errors: Show error, abort immediately
  • Exit code: Non-zero on any error

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Data validation pipelines
  • CI/CD quality gates
  • Critical processing where partial results aren't acceptable
  • Debugging log parsing issues

docs.title: Example Behavior
docs.text:
> kelora -j --strict app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int() * 2'

Input: 

{"value": "123"}
{"value": "invalid"}
{"value": "456"}

Output: 

result=246
⚠️  kelora: line 2: exec error - cannot convert 'invalid' to integer

Exit code: 1

Processing stops at the first error. Line 3 is never processed.

docs.title: Enabling Strict Mode
docs.text: > kelora -j --strict app.log

docs.title: Parse Errors
docs.text:
Occur when input lines can't be parsed in the specified format.

JSON parse error: 

> kelora -j app.log

Input: 

{"valid": "json"}
{invalid json}
{"more": "valid"}

Resilient behavior: - Line 1: Parsed successfully - Line 2: Skipped (parse error recorded) - Line 3: Parsed successfully

Strict behavior: - Line 1: Parsed successfully - Line 2: Error shown, processing aborts - Line 3: Never processed

docs.title: Filter Errors
docs.text:
Occur when --filter expressions fail during evaluation.

Example: 

> kelora -j --filter 'e.timestamp.to_unix() > 1000000' app.log

If e.timestamp is missing:

Resilient behavior: - Filter evaluates to false - Event is skipped - Error recorded

Strict behavior: - Error shown immediately - Processing aborts

docs.title: Transform Errors
docs.text:
Occur when --exec scripts fail during execution.

Example: 

> kelora -j --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int()' app.log

If e.value is not a valid integer:

Resilient behavior: - Transformation rolled back (atomic) - Original event returned unchanged - Error recorded

Strict behavior: - Error shown immediately - Processing aborts

docs.title: Default Error Reporting
docs.text:
By default, errors are collected and summarized at the end:

> kelora -j app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int()'

Summary: 

🔹 Processed 100 lines, 95 events output, 5 errors

docs.title: Verbose Mode (--verbose)
docs.text:
Show each error immediately as it occurs:

> kelora -j --verbose app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int()'

Output: 

⚠️  kelora: line 5: exec error - cannot convert 'abc' to integer
result=123
⚠️  kelora: line 12: exec error - cannot convert 'def' to integer
result=456
⚠️  kelora: line 23: exec error - field 'value' not found
result=789

Summary: 

🔹 Processed 100 lines, 95 events output, 5 errors

docs.title: Multiple Verbosity Levels
docs.text:
-v      # Show errors immediately
-vv     # Show errors with more context
-vvv    # Show errors with full details

docs.title: Verbose with Strict
docs.text:
Combine for immediate errors and fail-fast:

> kelora -j --strict --verbose app.log

Errors are shown immediately, then processing aborts.

docs.title: Graduated Quiet Levels
docs.text:
Suppress output for automation:

Level Effect -q Suppress diagnostics (errors, stats, context markers) -qq Additionally suppress event output (same as -F none) -qqq Additionally suppress script side effects (print(), eprint())

docs.title: Level 1: Suppress Diagnostics
docs.text:
> kelora -q -j app.log --stats
  • Errors not shown
  • Stats not shown
  • Events still output
  • Exit code indicates success/failure

docs.title: Level 2: Suppress Events
docs.text:
> kelora -qq -j app.log --exec 'track_count(e.service)' --metrics
  • Errors not shown
  • Events not shown
  • Metrics still shown (if --metrics)
  • Exit code indicates success/failure

docs.title: Level 3: Complete Silence
docs.text:
> kelora -qqq -j app.log
  • No output at all
  • Exit code is only indicator
  • Useful for validation pipelines
> kelora -qqq -j app.log && echo "Clean" || echo "Has errors"

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
Kelora uses standard Unix exit codes:

Code Meaning 0 Success (no errors) 1 Processing errors (parse/filter/exec errors) 2 Invalid usage (CLI errors, file not found) 130 Interrupted (Ctrl+C) 141 Broken pipe (normal in Unix pipelines)

docs.title: Using Exit Codes
docs.text:
In shell scripts: 

if kelora -q -j app.log; then
    echo "✓ No errors found"
else
    echo "✗ Errors detected"
    exit 1
fi

In CI/CD: 

kelora -qq --strict app.log || exit 1

With automation: 

kelora -qqq app.log; echo "Exit code: $?"

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
In resilient mode, --exec scripts execute atomically:

> kelora -j --exec 'e.a = 1; e.b = e.value.to_int(); e.c = 3' app.log

If e.value.to_int() fails: - Changes to e.a are rolled back - e.b is never set - e.c is never set - Original event is returned unchanged

docs.title: Why Atomic?
docs.text:
Prevents partial transformations from corrupting data:

Without atomicity: 

// Input
{"value": "invalid"}

// Broken output (partial transformation)
{"value": "invalid", "a": 1}  // Missing b and c!

With atomicity: 

// Input
{"value": "invalid"}

// Output (unchanged)
{"value": "invalid"}  // Clean original event

docs.title: Multiple --exec Scripts
docs.text:
Each --exec script is atomic independently:

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.a = e.x.to_int()' \
    --exec 'e.b = e.y.to_int()' \
    app.log

If first --exec fails: - First transformation rolled back - Second --exec still runs on original event

If second --exec fails: - First transformation preserved (it succeeded) - Second transformation rolled back

docs.title: Missing Fields
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --filter 'e.timestamp > "2024-01-01"' app.log

Some events missing timestamp field.

Solution: Use safe access: 

> kelora -j --filter 'e.has_path("timestamp") && e.timestamp > "2024-01-01"' app.log

docs.title: Type Mismatches
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --exec 'e.result = e.value * 2' app.log

e.value is a string, not a number.

Solution: Use type conversion with defaults: 

> kelora -j --exec 'e.result = to_int_or(e.value, 0) * 2' app.log

docs.title: Invalid Timestamps
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --filter 'e.timestamp.to_unix() > 1000000' app.log

e.timestamp is not a valid timestamp.

Solution: Use safe access: 

> kelora -j --filter 'e.has_path("timestamp") && e.timestamp.to_unix() > 1000000' app.log

docs.title: Array Index Out of Bounds
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --exec 'e.first = e.items[0]' app.log

e.items is empty or missing.

Solution: Check array length: 

> kelora -j --exec 'if e.has_path("items") && e.items.len() > 0 { e.first = e.items[0] }' app.log

docs.title: Division by Zero
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --exec 'e.ratio = e.success / e.total' app.log

e.total is zero.

Solution: Add guard: 

> kelora -j --exec 'if e.total > 0 { e.ratio = e.success / e.total } else { e.ratio = 0.0 }' app.log

docs.title: Use Verbose Mode
docs.text:
See errors as they happen:

> kelora -j --verbose app.log --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int()'

docs.title: Enable Strict Mode
docs.text:
Find first error quickly:

> kelora -j --strict app.log

docs.title: Inspect Problematic Lines
docs.text:
Use --take to limit processing:

> kelora -j --strict --take 100 app.log

Process only first 100 lines to find issues faster.

docs.title: Check Field Existence
docs.text:
Verify fields exist before accessing:

> kelora -j --exec 'if !e.has_path("value") { eprint("Line missing value: " + e) }' app.log

docs.title: Use Type Checking
docs.text:
Verify field types before operations:

> kelora -j --exec 'if type_of(e.value) != "i64" { eprint("Value is not integer: " + e.value) }' app.log

docs.title: Validate Input Format
docs.text:
Test parsing with strict mode:

> kelora -j --strict --stats-only app.log

No output, but exits with error if parsing fails.

docs.title: Parse Error Format
docs.text:
⚠️  kelora: line 42: parse error - invalid JSON at position 15
  • line 42: Line number in input
  • parse error: Error category
  • Details: Specific error message

docs.title: Filter Error Format
docs.text: ⚠️  kelora: line 42: filter error - field 'timestamp' not found

docs.title: Exec Error Format
docs.text: ⚠️  kelora: line 42: exec error - cannot convert 'abc' to integer

docs.title: Enhanced Error Summaries
docs.text:
With --verbose, get example errors:

🔹 Processed 1000 lines, 950 events output, 50 errors

Error examples:
  line 42: exec error - cannot convert 'abc' to integer
  line 103: exec error - field 'value' not found
  line 287: filter error - timestamp is null

docs.title: Use Resilient Mode for Production
docs.text:
Production logs are messy - resilient mode handles gracefully:

> kelora -j app.log --levels error --keys timestamp,message

docs.title: Use Strict Mode for Validation
docs.text:
Validate data quality in pipelines:

> kelora -j --strict app.log > /dev/null && echo "✓ Valid"

docs.title: Combine Quiet and Exit Codes
docs.text:
For automation, use exit codes:

> kelora -qq app.log
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "No errors"
else
    echo "Has errors"
fi

docs.title: Add Defensive Checks
docs.text:
Use safe field access patterns:

> kelora -j --exec 'e.result = e.get_path("nested.value", 0) * 2' app.log

docs.title: Log Errors to File
docs.text:
Capture errors for later analysis:

> kelora -j --verbose app.log 2> errors.log

docs.title: Use Stats for Summary
docs.text:
Get error counts without verbose output:

> kelora -j --stats app.log

Shows error count in summary.

docs.title: Error Handling in Parallel Mode
docs.text:
When using --parallel, error handling works the same:

> kelora -j --parallel app.log
  • Errors still recorded per event
  • Summary shows total errors across all threads
  • Exit code reflects any errors from any thread

docs.title: Verbose with Parallel
docs.text:
Verbose errors are shown immediately, but may be interleaved:

> kelora -j --parallel --verbose app.log

Errors from different threads may appear out of order.

docs.title: Strict with Parallel
docs.text:
First error from any thread aborts all processing:

> kelora -j --parallel --strict app.log

docs.title: Events and Fields
docs.text: Understanding how Kelora represents log data as structured events and how to access their fields.

docs.title: What is an Event?
docs.text:
An event is Kelora's internal representation of a single log entry. After parsing, each log line becomes an event (a map/object) with fields that you can access and transform.

// In Rhai scripts, the current event is available as 'e'
e.timestamp  // Access field directly
e.level      // Access another field
e.message    // And so on

docs.title: Event Structure
docs.text:
Events are maps (key-value pairs) where: - Keys are field names (strings) - Values can be any JSON-compatible type

{
  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "api",
  "user": {
    "id": 12345,
    "name": "alice"
  },
  "tags": ["authentication", "security"],
  "duration_ms": 1234
}

After parsing, this becomes an event with fields accessible as: - e.timestamp → "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z" - e.level → "ERROR" - e.service → "api" - e.user → Map with id and name fields - e.tags → Array ["authentication", "security"] - e.duration_ms → 1234

docs.title: Field Types
docs.text:
Kelora preserves JSON types after parsing:

Type Example Value Rhai Access String "error" e.level Integer 404 e.status Float 1.234 e.duration Boolean true e.success Null null e.optional_field → () Object/Map {"key": "value"} e.metadata Array [1, 2, 3] e.scores

Unit Type (): In Rhai, null from JSON becomes the unit type (), representing "no value" or "empty".

docs.title: Direct Access
docs.text:
For simple field names (alphanumeric, no special characters):

e.timestamp
e.level
e.service
e.user_id

docs.title: Nested Access
docs.text:
Access nested fields using dot notation:

e.user.name          // Object field
e.user.id            // Another nested field
e.metadata.region    // Deeper nesting

docs.title: Array Access
docs.text:
Access array elements by index:

e.tags[0]            // First element
e.tags[1]            // Second element
e.tags[-1]           // Last element (negative indexing)
e.tags[-2]           // Second-to-last element

docs.title: Bracket Notation
docs.text:
For field names with special characters or dynamic access:

e["content-type"]           // Hyphens in field name
e["@timestamp"]             // @ symbol in name
e["user-agent"]             // Multiple special chars
e.headers["authorization"]  // Nested with special chars

docs.title: Deep Nested Access
docs.text:
Combine patterns for complex structures:

e.user.addresses[0].city                    // Object → array → object
e.data.items[-1].metadata.tags[0]          // Multiple levels
e.response.headers["content-type"]          // Object → bracket notation

docs.title: Check Field Existence
docs.text:
Before accessing fields, check if they exist:

// Top-level field
if "field" in e {
    e.field
} else {
    "default"
}

// Nested field
if e.has_path("user.role") {
    e.user.role
} else {
    "guest"
}

docs.title: Array Bounds Checking
docs.text:
Check array length before accessing elements:

if e.scores.len() > 0 {
    e.scores[0]
} else {
    0
}

// Last element safely
if e.items.len() > 0 {
    e.items[-1]
} else {
    #{}
}

docs.title: Safe Path Access
docs.text:
Use get_path() for safe nested access with defaults:

// Returns default if path doesn't exist
e.user_role = e.get_path("user.role", "guest")
e.first_tag = e.get_path("tags[0]", "untagged")
e.response_code = e.get_path("response.status", 0)

// Complex nested paths
e.city = e.get_path("user.address.city", "unknown")

docs.title: Type Checking
docs.text:
Check if field has a value (not unit type):

if type_of(e.field) != "()" {
    // Field exists and has a value
    e.field
}

docs.title: Add Fields
docs.text:
Assign values to new or existing fields:

e.processed = true
e.category = "error"
e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000

docs.title: Modify Existing Fields
docs.text:
Transform field values in place:

e.level = e.level.to_upper()
e.message = e.message.trim()
e.tags = sorted(e.tags)

docs.title: Remove Fields
docs.text:
Assign unit () to remove fields:

e.password = ()          // Remove sensitive field
e.internal_id = ()       // Remove another field

Removed fields won't appear in output.

docs.title: Remove Entire Event
docs.text:
Clear all fields to filter out the event:

if e.level == "DEBUG" {
    e = ()  // Event becomes empty and is filtered out
}

Empty events are counted as "filtered" in statistics.

docs.title: Common Field Names
docs.text:
Kelora recognizes these standard field names across formats:

Timestamps: - timestamp, ts, time, @timestamp

Log Levels: - level, severity, loglevel

Messages: - message, msg, text

Identifiers: - id, request_id, trace_id, span_id

Metadata: - service, host, hostname, source

docs.title: Format-Specific Fields
docs.text:
Different parsers add format-specific fields:

JSON (-f json): - Preserves all original fields - Nested structures maintained

Syslog (-f syslog): - hostname, appname, procid, msgid - facility, severity

Combined/Apache (-f combined): - ip, timestamp, request, status, bytes - method, path, protocol - referer, user_agent - request_time (NGINX only)

CSV (-f csv): - Column names from header row - Or col_0, col_1, col_2, etc. without header

Logfmt (-f logfmt): - All key-value pairs as top-level fields

docs.title: Objects/Maps
docs.text:
Access nested maps using dot notation:

bash: line 1: kelora: command not found

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Process arrays with Rhai array functions:

> kelora -f json input.log \
    --exec 'e.tag_count = e.tags.len()' \
    --exec 'e.first_tag = e.get_path("tags[0]", "none")' \
    --exec 'e.unique_tags = unique(e.tags)' \
    --keys timestamp,tag_count,first_tag,unique_tags

docs.title: Fan-Out Arrays
docs.text:
Convert array elements to individual events:

> kelora -f json batch.log \
    --exec 'emit_each(e.items)' \
    --keys item_id,status

Each element in e.items becomes a separate event.

docs.title: Mixed Structures
docs.text:
Handle complex nested structures:

{
  "user": {
    "id": 12345,
    "scores": [85, 92, 78],
    "metadata": {
      "tags": ["premium", "verified"]
    }
  }
}

Access patterns:

e.user_id = e.user.id                           // Nested object
e.first_score = e.user.scores[0]                // Object → array
e.last_score = e.user.scores[-1]                // Negative index
e.avg_score = e.user.scores.sum() / e.user.scores.len()
e.first_tag = e.user.metadata.tags[0]           // Deep nesting
e.is_premium = "premium" in e.user.metadata.tags // Array membership

docs.title: Output Format: Bracket Notation
docs.text:
The default formatter uses bracket notation for arrays:

scores[0]=85 scores[1]=92 scores[2]=78
user.name=alice user.scores[0]=85
items[0].id=1 items[0].status=active

This matches the path syntax used in get_path():

// Access and path syntax are consistent
e.get_path("scores[0]", 0)           // Access first score
e.get_path("items[1].status", "")    // Access nested array element

docs.title: Field Selection: Top-Level Only
docs.text:
The --keys parameter operates on top-level fields only:

# ✅ Supported: Select top-level fields
> kelora -f json input.log --keys user,timestamp,message

# ❌ Not supported: Nested paths in --keys
> kelora -f json input.log --keys user.name,scores[0]

To extract nested fields, use --exec to promote them to top-level:

> kelora -f json input.log \
    --exec 'e.user_name = e.get_path("user.name", "")' \
    --exec 'e.first_score = e.get_path("scores[0]", 0)' \
    --keys user_name,first_score

docs.title: Extract Nested Fields
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.user_name = e.get_path("user.name", "unknown")' \
    --exec 'e.user_role = e.get_path("user.role", "guest")' \
    --keys timestamp,user_name,user_role

docs.title: Flatten Structures
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.request_method = e.request.method' \
    --exec 'e.request_path = e.request.path' \
    --exec 'e.request = ()' \
    --keys timestamp,request_method,request_path

docs.title: Combine Fields
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.full_name = e.first_name + " " + e.last_name' \
    --exec 'e.endpoint = e.method + " " + e.path' \
    --keys timestamp,full_name,endpoint

docs.title: Conditional Field Creation
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'if e.status >= 500 { e.severity = "critical" } else if e.status >= 400 { e.severity = "warning" } else { e.severity = "normal" }' \
    --keys timestamp,status,severity

docs.title: Array Transformations
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.tag_count = e.tags.len()' \
    --exec 'e.sorted_tags = sorted(e.tags)' \
    --exec 'e.unique_tags = unique(e.tags)' \
    --keys timestamp,tag_count,sorted_tags

docs.title: Safe Deep Access
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.city = e.get_path("user.address.city", "N/A")' \
    --exec 'e.zip = e.get_path("user.address.zip", "00000")' \
    --exec 'e.country = e.get_path("user.address.country", "Unknown")' \
    --keys city,zip,country

docs.title: String to Number
docs.text:
e.status_code = e.status.to_int()           // String to integer
e.duration = e.duration_str.to_float()      // String to float

With defaults if conversion fails:

e.status_code = to_int_or(e.status, 0)
e.duration = to_float_or(e.duration_str, 0.0)

docs.title: Number to String
docs.text:
e.status_str = e.status.to_string()
e.duration_str = e.duration.to_string()

docs.title: Boolean Conversions
docs.text:
e.is_error = to_bool(e.error_flag)          // "true"/"false" to boolean
e.success = to_bool_or(e.status_ok, false)  // With default

docs.title: Type Checking
docs.text:
e.field_type = type_of(e.field)

// Common checks
if type_of(e.field) == "i64" { /* integer */ }
if type_of(e.field) == "f64" { /* float */ }
if type_of(e.field) == "string" { /* string */ }
if type_of(e.field) == "array" { /* array */ }
if type_of(e.field) == "map" { /* object/map */ }
if type_of(e.field) == "()" { /* null/empty */ }

docs.title: Direct vs Path Access
docs.text:
Direct access is fastest: 

e.level           // Fast: direct map lookup
e.user.name       // Fast: two map lookups

Path access is more flexible but slightly slower: 

e.get_path("level", "INFO")              // Parses path string
e.get_path("user.name", "unknown")       // More overhead

Use direct access when field names are known and simple.

docs.title: Field Existence Checks
docs.text:
Fastest - direct membership: 

"field" in e

Flexible - path checking: 

e.has_path("user.role")
e.has_path("items[0].status")

docs.title: Array Operations
docs.text:
Array functions create new arrays (not in-place):

// Creates new sorted array
e.sorted_scores = sorted(e.scores)

// Original array unchanged
e.scores  // Still unsorted

For large arrays, avoid unnecessary transformations.

docs.title: Field Not Found
docs.text:
Problem: Accessing non-existent field causes error.

Solution: Use safe access patterns: 

// Check before access
if "field" in e {
    e.field
}

// Use get_path with default
e.get_path("field", "default")

docs.title: Array Index Out of Bounds
docs.text:
Problem: Accessing array element beyond length.

Solution: Check array length first: 

if e.items.len() > 5 {
    e.items[5]
}

// Or use safe path access
e.get_path("items[5]", #{})

docs.title: Type Mismatch
docs.text:
Problem: Field has unexpected type.

Solution: Use type conversion with defaults: 

e.status_code = to_int_or(e.status, 0)
e.duration = to_float_or(e.duration_ms, 0.0)

docs.title: Nested Field Changes Not Persisting
docs.text:
Problem: Modifying nested fields doesn't work as expected.

Solution: Reassign the parent object: 

// This might not work
e.user.name = "alice"

// Do this instead
let user = e.user;
user.name = "alice";
e.user = user;

docs.title: Field Name with Special Characters
docs.text:
Problem: Field names contain hyphens, dots, or other special chars.

Solution: Use bracket notation: 

e["content-type"]
e["user-agent"]
e["@timestamp"]

docs.title: Pipeline Model
docs.text: Understanding how Kelora processes logs through a multi-stage pipeline.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kelora processes logs through a streaming pipeline with distinct stages. Each stage transforms the data and passes it to the next stage. Understanding this model helps you write more effective log processing commands.

docs.title: Pipeline Stages
docs.text: Input → Parse → Filter → Transform → Output

docs.title: 1. Input Stage
docs.text:
Purpose: Read and preprocess log lines from files or stdin.

Operations: - Read files (including .gz compressed) - Handle stdin from pipes - Split into lines - Skip empty lines (except -f line format) - Apply --extract-prefix if configured

Key Flags: - Files specified as positional arguments - --extract-prefix - Extract prefixed text before parsing - --prefix-sep - Separator for prefix extraction

Example: 

> kelora file1.log file2.log.gz
> tail -f app.log | kelora -j
> docker compose logs | kelora --extract-prefix service

docs.title: 2. Parse Stage
docs.text:
Purpose: Convert raw log lines into structured events (maps/objects).

Operations: - Detect or apply format (-f json, -f logfmt, etc.) - Parse line into fields - Handle parse errors (skip in resilient mode, abort in strict mode) - Apply --ts-format and --input-tz for timestamps

Key Flags: - -f, --input-format - Specify format (json, logfmt, syslog, combined, etc.) - --ts-format - Custom timestamp format - --input-tz - Timezone for naive timestamps - --strict - Fail on parse errors

Example: 

> kelora -f json app.log
> kelora -f combined access.log
> kelora -f "cols:timestamp:ts level:5 message:*" custom.log

Output: Structured event (map) with fields accessible as e.field.

docs.title: 3. Filter Stage
docs.text:
Purpose: Select which events to process further.

Operations: - Level filtering (--levels) - Time filtering (--since, --until) - Custom Rhai expressions (--filter) - Context lines (--before-context, --after-context)

Key Flags: - --levels - Filter by log level - --since / --until - Time-based filtering - --filter - Custom Rhai expression (must return true/false) - --before-context / --after-context - Include surrounding events

Execution Order: 1. Level filtering 2. Time filtering 3. Custom filters (each --filter in order) 4. Context lines (if matched)

Example: 

> kelora -j app.log --levels error
> kelora -j app.log --since "1 hour ago"
> kelora -j app.log --filter 'e.service == "database"'

Behavior: - Filters return true (keep) or false (skip) - In resilient mode: filter errors return false - In strict mode: filter errors abort processing

docs.title: 4. Transform Stage
docs.text:
Purpose: Modify, enrich, or aggregate event data.

Operations: - Execute Rhai scripts (--exec) - Run --begin scripts once at start - Run --end scripts once at finish - Track metrics (track_count(), etc.) - Fan-out arrays (emit_each()) - Remove fields (e.field = ())

Key Flags: - --begin - Run once before processing - --exec - Run for each event (multiple allowed) - --end - Run once after processing - --metrics - Display tracked metrics at end - --window - Enable windowed analysis

Execution Order: 1. --begin (once, before any events) 2. For each event: - Execute each --exec in order - Atomic execution (rollback on error in resilient mode) 3. --end (once, after all events) 4. Display --metrics (if enabled)

Example: 

> kelora -j app.log \
    --begin 'print("Starting analysis")' \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'print("Complete")' \
    --metrics

Behavior: - Transformations modify events in place - In resilient mode: errors return original event unchanged - In strict mode: transformation errors abort processing - Empty events (e = ()) are filtered out before output

docs.title: 5. Output Stage
docs.text:
Purpose: Format and emit events.

Operations: - Apply --keys field selection - Convert timestamps (--convert-ts, --show-ts-local, --show-ts-utc) - Format events (default, JSON, CSV, etc.) - Apply --take limit - Write to stdout or files

Key Flags: - --keys - Select top-level fields to output - -F, --output-format - Output format (default, json, csv, etc.) - --convert-ts - Convert timestamp fields to RFC3339 - --show-ts-local / --show-ts-utc - Display timestamp format - --take - Limit output to N events

Example: 

> kelora -j app.log --keys timestamp,service,message
> kelora -j app.log -F json
> kelora -j app.log --take 100

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Kelora processes events one at a time (or in batches with --parallel):

  • Low memory usage - Events are processed and discarded
  • Real-time processing - Works with tail -f and live streams
  • No lookahead - Can't access future events (except with --window)

docs.title: Sequential vs Parallel
docs.text:
Sequential (default): - Events processed in order - Lower memory usage - Predictable output order - Simpler debugging

Parallel (--parallel): - Events processed in batches across cores - Higher throughput - May reorder output (use --ordered to preserve) - Higher memory usage

docs.title: Event Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Line read from input
2. Line parsed into event map
3. Event passes through filters
4. Event transformed by --exec scripts
5. Event formatted and output
6. Event discarded (unless windowed)

docs.title: Simple Filter-and-Select
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log \
    --filter 'e.level == "ERROR"' \
    --keys timestamp,service,message

Pipeline: Input → Parse → Filter → Output (with field selection)

docs.title: Filter-Transform-Output
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log \
    --filter 'e.service == "api"' \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --keys timestamp,duration_s,path

Pipeline: Input → Parse → Filter → Transform → Output

docs.title: Aggregate and Report
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --exec 'track_avg("response_time", e.duration_ms)' \
    --metrics \
    -F none

Pipeline: Input → Parse → Transform (tracking) → Output (metrics only)

docs.title: Multi-Stage Filtering
docs.text:
> kelora -j app.log \
    --levels error,warn \
    --since "1 hour ago" \
    --filter 'e.service != "health-check"' \
    --keys timestamp,level,service,message

Pipeline: Input → Parse → Filter (levels) → Filter (time) → Filter (custom) → Output

docs.title: Fan-Out Processing
docs.text:
> kelora -j batch.log \
    --exec 'emit_each(e.items, #{batch_id: e.batch_id})' \
    --filter 'e.status == "active"' \
    --keys batch_id,item_id,status

Pipeline: Input → Parse → Transform (fan-out) → Filter → Output

docs.title: Resilient Mode (Default)
docs.text:
• Parse errors: Skip line, continue processing
  • Filter errors: Treat as false, skip event
  • Transform errors: Return original event, continue
  • Summary: Show error count at end

docs.title: Strict Mode (--strict)
docs.text:
• Parse errors: Show error, abort immediately
  • Filter errors: Show error, abort immediately
  • Transform errors: Show error, abort immediately
  • Summary: No summary (aborted)

docs.title: Verbose Mode (--verbose)
docs.text:
• Shows each error immediately as it occurs
  • Works in both resilient and strict modes
  • Useful for debugging pipeline issues

docs.title: Stateless Processing
docs.text: Most operations are stateless: - Each event processed independently - No memory of previous events - Can process infinite streams

docs.title: Stateful Features
docs.text:
Some features maintain state:

Metrics Tracking: 

> kelora -j app.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --metrics

Maintains counters in memory.

Window Functions: 

> kelora -j app.log \
    --window 5 \
    --exec 'e.recent = window_values("status")'

Maintains sliding window of recent events.

Context Lines: 

> kelora -j app.log \
    --filter 'e.level == "ERROR"' \
    --before-context 2

Buffers events to provide context.

docs.title: Early Filtering
docs.text:
Place cheap filters early to reduce work:

# Good: Level filter before expensive regex
> kelora -j app.log \
    --levels error \
    --filter 'e.message.has_matches(r"complex.*pattern")'

# Less efficient: Expensive filter on all events
> kelora -j app.log \
    --filter 'e.message.has_matches(r"complex.*pattern")' \
    --filter 'e.level == "ERROR"'

docs.title: Selective Field Access
docs.text:
Use --keys to reduce output processing:

> kelora -j app.log \
    --keys timestamp,message \
    -F json

docs.title: Parallel Processing
docs.text:
Use --parallel for CPU-bound transformations:

> kelora -j large.log \
    --parallel \
    --exec 'e.hash = e.content.hash("sha256")' \
    --batch-size 1000

docs.title: Limiting Output
docs.text:
Use --take for quick exploration:

> kelora -j large.log --take 100

docs.title: Scripting Stages
docs.text: Deep dive into Kelora's three Rhai scripting stages: --begin, --exec, and --end.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Kelora provides three scripting stages for transforming log data with Rhai scripts:

--begin  →  [Process Events]  →  --end
              ↓
           --exec (per event)
Stage Runs Purpose Access --begin Once before processing Initialize state, load data conf map, file helpers --exec Once per event Transform events e (event), conf, tracking --end Once after processing Summarize, report metrics, conf

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The --begin stage runs once before any events are processed. Use it to:

  • Initialize lookup tables
  • Load reference data from files
  • Set up shared configuration
  • Prepare the conf map for use in other stages

docs.title: The conf Map
docs.text:
The global conf map is read-write in --begin and read-only in later stages.

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.valid_users = ["alice", "bob", "charlie"]' \
    --exec 'e.is_valid = e.user in conf.valid_users' \
    app.log

docs.title: Available Helpers
docs.text: Special functions available only in --begin:

docs.title: read_lines(path)
docs.text:
Read file as array of strings (one per line, UTF-8).

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.blocked_ips = read_lines("blocked.txt")' \
    --exec 'if e.ip in conf.blocked_ips { e = () }' \
    app.log

docs.title: read_file(path)
docs.text:
Read entire file as single string (UTF-8).

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.template = read_file("template.txt")' \
    --end 'print(conf.template.replace("{count}", metrics["total"].to_string()))' \
    app.log

docs.title: read_json(path)
docs.text:
Parse JSON file (convenience helper).

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.users = read_json("users.json")' \
    --exec 'e.user_name = conf.users.get(e.user_id, "unknown")' \
    app.log

docs.title: Load Lookup Table
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.services = #{api: "API Gateway", db: "Database", cache: "Redis"}' \
    --exec 'e.service_name = conf.services.get(e.service, e.service)' \
    app.log

docs.title: Load IP Geolocation Data
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.ip_to_country = read_json("geoip.json")' \
    --exec 'e.country = conf.ip_to_country.get(e.ip, "unknown")' \
    app.log

docs.title: Initialize Counters
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.start_time = now_utc()' \
    --end 'let duration = now_utc() - conf.start_time; print("Processed in " + duration + "s")' \
    app.log

docs.title: Load Configuration
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.threshold = 1000; conf.alert_email = "ops@company.com"' \
    --exec 'if e.duration_ms > conf.threshold { eprint("⚠️  Slow request: " + e.path) }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The --exec stage runs once per event. Use it to:

  • Transform event fields
  • Add computed fields
  • Filter events (via e = ())
  • Track metrics
  • Emit multiple events from arrays

docs.title: The Event Variable
docs.text:
The current event is available as e. Modifications to e persist through subsequent --exec scripts.

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --exec 'e.is_slow = e.duration_s > 1.0' \
    app.log

docs.title: Multiple Exec Scripts
docs.text:
Multiple --exec scripts run in order. Each sees changes from previous scripts.

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --exec 'track_avg("duration", e.duration_s)' \
    --exec 'if e.duration_s > 5.0 { e.alert = true }' \
    app.log

Execution order: 1. Convert duration_ms to duration_s 2. Track average duration 3. Add alert field for slow requests

docs.title: Atomic Execution
docs.text:
In resilient mode (default), exec scripts execute atomically:

  • If an error occurs, changes are rolled back
  • Original event is returned unchanged
  • Processing continues with next event
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.result = e.value.to_int() * 2' \
    app.log

If e.value is not a valid integer: - Error is recorded - Event passes through unchanged - No partial modifications

In strict mode (--strict), errors abort immediately.

docs.title: Transform Fields
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.level = e.level.to_upper()' \
    --exec 'e.message = e.message.trim()' \
    app.log

docs.title: Add Computed Fields
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --exec 'e.timestamp_unix = e.timestamp.to_unix()' \
    app.log

docs.title: Conditional Field Creation
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'if e.status >= 500 { e.severity = "critical" } else if e.status >= 400 { e.severity = "error" }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Remove Events
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'if e.level == "DEBUG" { e = () }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Track Metrics
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --exec 'track_avg("response_time", e.duration_ms)' \
    --metrics \
    app.log

docs.title: Fan-Out Arrays
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'emit_each(e.items)' \
    app.log

Each array element becomes a separate event.

docs.title: Access to conf
docs.text:
The conf map from --begin is read-only in --exec:

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.multiplier = 2.5' \
    --exec 'e.adjusted = e.value * conf.multiplier' \
    app.log

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The --end stage runs once after all events are processed. Use it to:

  • Summarize metrics
  • Generate reports
  • Print final statistics
  • Export aggregated data

docs.title: The metrics Map
docs.text:
The global metrics map contains all tracked data from track_*() functions:

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'for key in metrics.keys() { print(key + ": " + metrics[key]) }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Available Data
docs.text:
In --end, you have access to:

  • metrics - All tracked metrics (counts, sums, averages, etc.)
  • conf - Read-only configuration from --begin
  • Standard Rhai functions (print, file helpers if --allow-fs-writes)

docs.title: Print Summary Statistics
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count("total"); if e.level == "ERROR" { track_count("errors") }' \
    --end 'let error_rate = metrics.errors / metrics.total * 100; print("Error rate: " + error_rate + "%")' \
    app.log

docs.title: Generate Report
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'print("=== Service Report ==="); for svc in metrics.keys() { print(svc + ": " + metrics[svc] + " requests") }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Export Metrics to File
docs.text:
> kelora -j --allow-fs-writes \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'append_file("report.txt", "Total services: " + metrics.len().to_string())' \
    app.log

docs.title: Calculate Percentages
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count("total"); track_count(e.level)' \
    --end 'for level in ["INFO", "WARN", "ERROR"] { let pct = metrics.get(level, 0) / metrics.total * 100; print(level + ": " + pct + "%") }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Data Flow Between Stages
docs.text:
--begin:  Initialize conf map
    ↓
    conf (read-only)
    ↓
--exec:   Process events, track metrics
    ↓
    metrics + conf (both read-only)
    ↓
--end:    Summarize and report

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.threshold = 1000; conf.start = now_utc()' \
    --exec 'if e.duration_ms > conf.threshold { track_count("slow") }' \
    --exec 'track_count("total")' \
    --end 'let elapsed = now_utc() - conf.start; print("Processed " + metrics.total + " events in " + elapsed + "s"); print("Slow requests: " + metrics.get("slow", 0))' \
    app.log

Flow: 1. --begin: Set threshold to 1000ms, record start time 2. --exec (per event): Track slow requests, track total 3. --end: Calculate elapsed time, print summary

docs.title: -E, --exec-file
docs.text:
Load Rhai script from file for the exec stage:

transform.rhai: 

// Convert duration to seconds
e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000;

// Add severity based on status
if e.status >= 500 {
    e.severity = "critical";
} else if e.status >= 400 {
    e.severity = "error";
} else {
    e.severity = "ok";
}

// Track metrics
track_count(e.severity);
track_avg("response_time", e.duration_s);

Usage: 

> kelora -j -E transform.rhai --metrics app.log

docs.title: -I, --include
docs.text:
Include Rhai library files before script stages:

helpers.rhai: 

fn classify_status(status) {
    if status >= 500 {
        "server_error"
    } else if status >= 400 {
        "client_error"
    } else if status >= 300 {
        "redirect"
    } else if status >= 200 {
        "success"
    } else {
        "other"
    }
}

Usage: 

> kelora -j \
    -I helpers.rhai \
    --exec 'e.status_class = classify_status(e.status)' \
    app.log

docs.title: Use --begin for Initialization
docs.text:
Good: 

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.lookup = read_json("data.json")' \
    --exec 'e.name = conf.lookup.get(e.id, "unknown")' \
    app.log

Bad: 

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'let lookup = read_json("data.json"); e.name = lookup.get(e.id, "unknown")' \
    app.log

The bad example reads the file once per event (slow and wasteful).

docs.title: Keep --exec Scripts Simple
docs.text:
Break complex logic into multiple --exec scripts:

Good: 

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --exec 'e.is_slow = e.duration_s > 1.0' \
    --exec 'if e.is_slow { track_count("slow_requests") }' \
    app.log

Bad: 

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000; e.is_slow = e.duration_s > 1.0; if e.is_slow { track_count("slow_requests") }' \
    app.log

The good example is easier to read and debug.

docs.title: Use --end for Summaries
docs.text:
Good: 

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'print("Total services: " + metrics.len())' \
    app.log

Bad: 

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service); print("Processing...")' \
    app.log

The bad example prints on every event (noisy).

docs.title: Leverage File Helpers
docs.text:
For complex logic, use -E and -I:

> kelora -j -I helpers.rhai -E transform.rhai --metrics app.log

This keeps command lines clean and logic maintainable.

docs.title: Begin Stage Overhead
docs.text:
The --begin stage runs once, so file I/O here is acceptable:

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.large_dataset = read_json("10mb.json")' \
    --exec 'e.enriched = conf.large_dataset.get(e.id, #{})' \
    app.log

docs.title: Exec Stage Optimization
docs.text:
The --exec stage runs per event. Avoid expensive operations:

Slow: 

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'let lookup = read_json("data.json"); e.name = lookup.get(e.id, "unknown")' \
    app.log

Fast: 

> kelora -j \
    --begin 'conf.lookup = read_json("data.json")' \
    --exec 'e.name = conf.lookup.get(e.id, "unknown")' \
    app.log

docs.title: End Stage Overhead
docs.text:
The --end stage runs once, so complex calculations are fine:

> kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'let sorted = metrics.keys().sort(); for key in sorted { print(key + ": " + metrics[key]) }' \
    app.log

docs.title: Parallel Processing
docs.text: When using --parallel, scripting stages behave differently:

docs.title: Begin and End
docs.text:
--begin and --end run once (not parallelized):

> kelora -j --parallel \
    --begin 'conf.start = now_utc()' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --end 'print("Duration: " + (now_utc() - conf.start))' \
    app.log

docs.title: Exec Stage
docs.text:
--exec runs in parallel across worker threads:

  • Each thread has its own copy of conf (read-only)
  • Tracking functions aggregate across threads
  • Event modifications are isolated per thread
> kelora -j --parallel \
    --exec 'e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    app.log

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text:
Kelora handles thread safety automatically:

  • conf is cloned per thread (immutable)
  • metrics uses thread-safe aggregation
  • Event modifications are isolated

You don't need to worry about race conditions in scripts.

docs.title: conf is Read-Only in --exec
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --exec 'conf.value = 42' app.log
# Error: conf is read-only in exec stage

Solution: Initialize in --begin: 

> kelora -j --begin 'conf.value = 42' --exec 'e.result = conf.value * 2' app.log

docs.title: metrics Not Available in --exec
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --exec 'print(metrics["total"])' app.log
# Error: metrics not available in exec stage

Solution: Use --end: 

> kelora -j --exec 'track_count("total")' --end 'print(metrics["total"])' app.log

docs.title: File Helpers Not Working
docs.text:
Problem: 

> kelora -j --exec 'append_file("out.txt", e.message)' app.log
# Error: filesystem writes not allowed

Solution: Add --allow-fs-writes: 

> kelora -j --allow-fs-writes --exec 'append_file("out.txt", e.message)' app.log

docs.title: Script Execution Order
docs.text:
Problem: Later --exec doesn't see earlier changes.

Check: Are you using --filter between them?

# This works - both --exec scripts run on same events
> kelora -j --exec 'e.a = 1' --exec 'e.b = e.a + 1' app.log

# This doesn't - filter may remove events before second --exec
> kelora -j --exec 'e.a = 1' --filter 'e.level == "ERROR"' --exec 'e.b = e.a + 1' app.log

Filters run between exec stages in the pipeline.

docs.title: Analyze Web Traffic
docs.text: Parse and analyze Apache/Nginx access logs to find slow requests, errors, and traffic patterns.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You have Apache or Nginx access logs and need to find slow requests, 4xx/5xx errors, traffic patterns, or analyze request distribution.

docs.title: Basic Combined Log Parsing
docs.text:
Parse Apache/Nginx combined format logs:

> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log --take 5

The combined format includes: ip, timestamp, request, method, path, protocol, status, bytes, referer, user_agent, and optionally request_time.

docs.title: Find Server Errors (5xx)
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.status >= 500' \
    --keys ip,timestamp,status,request

docs.title: Find Client Errors (4xx)
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400 && e.status < 500' \
    --keys ip,timestamp,status,request

docs.title: Find Slow Requests
docs.text:
For Nginx logs with request_time:

> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.get_path("request_time", "0").to_float() > 1.0' \
    --keys ip,request,request_time,status

docs.title: Traffic by Status Code
docs.text:
Count requests by status code:

> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.status)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Top IPs by Request Count
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.ip)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Analyze Specific Endpoints
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.path.contains("/api/")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.path)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Find Suspicious Activity
docs.text:
Look for unusual patterns:

# High request rates from single IP
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.ip)' \
    --metrics

# POST requests to unusual paths
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.method == "POST" && !e.path.starts_with("/api/")' \
    --keys ip,timestamp,method,path

# Large response sizes
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.get_path("bytes", "0").to_int() > 10000000' \
    --keys ip,path,bytes,timestamp

docs.title: Time-Based Analysis
docs.text:
Analyze traffic in specific time windows:

# Last hour's errors
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --since "1 hour ago" \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400'

# Traffic during specific time range
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --since "2024-01-15 09:00:00" \
    --until "2024-01-15 17:00:00" \
    --exec 'track_count(e.status)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Response Time Percentiles
docs.text:
Calculate performance metrics for Nginx logs with request_time:

> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --exec 'track_bucket("latency", floor(e.get_path("request_time", "0").to_float() * 1000 / 100) * 100)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Daily Error Report
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log* \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400' \
    --exec 'e.hour = e.timestamp.extract_re(r"(\d{2}):\d{2}:\d{2}", 1)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.hour)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.status)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: API Endpoint Performance
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.path.starts_with("/api/")' \
    --exec 'e.endpoint = e.path.extract_re(r"(/api/[^/]+)", 1)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.endpoint)' \
    --exec 'track_avg(e.endpoint, e.get_path("request_time", "0").to_float())' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Bot Detection
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.user_agent.contains("bot") || e.user_agent.contains("crawler")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.user_agent)' \
    --keys ip,user_agent,path \
    --metrics

docs.title: Referer Analysis
docs.text:
Find where traffic is coming from:

> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.referer != "-" && !e.referer.contains("yourdomain.com")' \
    --exec 'e.domain = e.referer.extract_domain()' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.domain)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Failed Authentication Attempts
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.path.contains("/login") && e.status == 401' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.ip)' \
    --keys timestamp,ip,path,status \
    --metrics

docs.title: Response Size Distribution
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --exec 'e.size_kb = floor(e.get_path("bytes", "0").to_int() / 1024)' \
    --exec 'track_bucket("response_size_kb", e.size_kb)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Export to CSV
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --keys ip,timestamp,status,bytes,request \
    -F csv > access.csv

docs.title: Export to JSON
docs.text:
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400' \
    -F json > errors.json

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
Large Files: 

# Use parallel processing
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log.* \
    --parallel \
    --filter 'e.status >= 500'

# Limit output
> kelora -f combined access.log --take 1000

Gzipped Archives: 

# Kelora handles .gz automatically
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log.*.gz \
    --filter 'e.status >= 500'

Multiple Files: 

# Process all access logs
> kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log* \
    --exec 'track_count(e.status)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text:
Find top N IPs by error count: 

> kelora -f combined access.log \
    --filter 'e.status >= 400' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.ip)' \
    --metrics

Hourly request distribution: 

> kelora -f combined access.log \
    --exec 'e.hour = e.timestamp.extract_re(r"(\d{2}):\d{2}:\d{2}", 1)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.hour)' \
    --metrics

Method distribution: 

> kelora -f combined access.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.method)' \
    --metrics

Status code summary: 

> kelora -f combined access.log \
    --exec 'e.status_class = floor(e.status / 100) + "xx"' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.status_class)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Timestamp parsing issues: 

# If timestamps aren't parsed, try explicit format
> kelora -f combined --ts-format "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z" access.log

Missing request_time field: 

# Apache combined format doesn't include request_time
# Only Nginx with custom log format includes it
# Use safe access with get_path()
e.get_path("request_time", "0")

Large numbers in bytes field: 

# Convert to MB for readability
e.bytes_mb = e.get_path("bytes", "0").to_float() / 1024 / 1024

docs.title: Find Errors in Logs
docs.text: Quickly find and analyze error-level events across different log formats.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You need to find error-level events in your logs, possibly across multiple files or formats, and understand what's happening around them.

docs.title: Basic Error Filtering
docs.text:
Filter by log level using --levels:

# JSON logs
kelora -f json app.log --levels error

# Logfmt logs
kelora -f logfmt service.log --levels error,critical

# Multiple levels (error, warn, critical)
kelora -f json app.log --levels warn,error

docs.title: Errors from Specific Time Range
docs.text:
Combine level filtering with time bounds:

# Errors from the last hour
kelora -f json app.log --levels error --since "1 hour ago"

# Errors in specific date range
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --since "2024-01-15 09:00:00" \
  --until "2024-01-15 17:00:00"

# Today's errors only
kelora -f json app.log --levels error --since "today"

docs.title: Errors from Specific Services
docs.text:
Use --filter for fine-grained control:

# Errors from database service only
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --filter 'e.service == "database"'

# Errors matching specific pattern
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --filter 'e.message.contains("timeout")'

# Errors with high severity
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --filter 'e.get_path("severity", 0) >= 8'

docs.title: Context Lines
docs.text:
Show surrounding events for context (like grep -A/-B/-C):

# Show 2 lines after each error
kelora -f json app.log --levels error --after-context 2

# Show 1 line before each error
kelora -f json app.log --levels error --before-context 1

# Show 2 lines before and after each error
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --before-context 2 --after-context 2

docs.title: Extract Key Fields
docs.text:
Focus on relevant information:

# Show only timestamp, service, and message
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --keys timestamp,service,message

# Include error code if present
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --exec 'e.error_code = e.get_path("error.code", "unknown")' \
  --keys timestamp,service,error_code,message

docs.title: Multiple Files
docs.text:
Search across many log files:

# All logs in directory
kelora -f json logs/*.jsonl --levels error

# Recursive search with find
find /var/log -name "*.log" -exec kelora -f auto {} --levels error \;

# Gzipped archives
kelora -f json logs/2024-01-*.log.gz --levels error

docs.title: Extract Error Patterns
docs.text:
Identify error codes and patterns:

# Extract error codes using regex
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --exec 'e.error_code = e.message.extract_re(r"ERR-(\d+)", 1)' \
  --keys timestamp,error_code,message

# Count error types
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --exec 'track_count(e.get_path("error.type", "unknown"))' \
  --metrics

docs.title: Output to Different Format
docs.text:
Export errors for further analysis:

# JSON output
kelora -f logfmt app.log --levels error -F json > errors.json

# CSV for spreadsheets
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --keys timestamp,service,message -F csv > errors.csv

docs.title: Find Database Errors
docs.text:
kelora -f json db.log --levels error \
  --filter 'e.message.contains("deadlock") || e.message.contains("constraint")' \
  --keys timestamp,query,error_message

docs.title: API Errors with Status Codes
docs.text:
kelora -f combined /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  --filter 'e.status >= 500' \
  --keys ip,timestamp,status,request,user_agent

docs.title: Application Crashes
docs.text:
kelora -f json app.log --levels error,critical \
  --filter 'e.message.contains("panic") || e.message.contains("fatal")' \
  --before-context 5 --after-context 2

docs.title: Errors by Hour
docs.text:
kelora -f json app.log --levels error \
  --exec 'e.hour = e.timestamp.format("%Y-%m-%d %H:00")' \
  --exec 'track_count(e.hour)' \
  --metrics

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
Performance: - Use --levels instead of --filter when possible (faster) - Add --parallel for large files - Use --take 100 to limit output when exploring

Debugging: - Use --verbose to see parsing errors - Use --stats to see processing summary - Use -F json | jq for complex JSON analysis

Automation: 

# Alert on errors (exit code 0 = no errors, 1 = has errors)
if kelora -q -f json app.log --levels error --since "5 minutes ago"; then
    echo "No errors found"
else
    echo "Errors detected!" | mail -s "Alert" admin@example.com
fi

docs.title: Monitor Application Health
docs.text: Extract health metrics and track service behavior from JSON application logs.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You have JSON logs from microservices and need to monitor health, track errors, measure performance, and understand service behavior.

docs.title: Basic Health Check
docs.text:
Monitor overall service health:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Error Rate Monitoring
docs.text:
Track error rates over time:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'if e.level == "ERROR" || e.level == "CRITICAL" { track_count("errors") }' \
    --exec 'track_count("total")' \
    --metrics

Calculate error percentage from metrics output.

docs.title: Service-Specific Health
docs.text:
Monitor individual service health:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.service == "database"' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --exec 'track_avg("duration", e.get_path("duration_ms", 0))' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Response Time Monitoring
docs.text:
Track performance metrics:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.has_path("duration_ms")' \
    --exec 'track_avg("response_time", e.duration_ms)' \
    --exec 'track_min("fastest", e.duration_ms)' \
    --exec 'track_max("slowest", e.duration_ms)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Memory Usage Tracking
docs.text:
Monitor memory consumption:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.has_path("memory_percent")' \
    --exec 'track_avg("memory", e.memory_percent)' \
    --exec 'track_max("peak_memory", e.memory_percent)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Endpoint Performance
docs.text:
Analyze API endpoint health:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.has_path("path")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.path)' \
    --exec 'track_avg(e.path, e.get_path("duration_ms", 0))' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Service Status Dashboard
docs.text:
Generate a comprehensive health report:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --exec 'if e.level == "ERROR" { track_count(e.service + "_errors") }' \
    --exec 'if e.has_path("duration_ms") { track_avg("avg_duration", e.duration_ms) }' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Failed Operations
docs.text:
Track operations that fail:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.get_path("status", "success") != "success"' \
    --exec 'e.operation = e.get_path("operation", "unknown")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.operation)' \
    --keys timestamp,service,operation,message \
    --metrics

docs.title: Database Query Health
docs.text:
Monitor database performance:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.service == "database"' \
    --exec 'if e.get_path("duration_ms", 0) > 1000 { e.slow = true }' \
    --exec 'track_count("queries")' \
    --exec 'if e.slow { track_count("slow_queries") }' \
    --exec 'track_avg("query_time", e.get_path("duration_ms", 0))' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Authentication Failures
docs.text:
Track login and auth issues:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.service == "auth"' \
    --filter 'e.message.contains("failed") || e.message.contains("locked")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.username)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.get_path("ip", "unknown"))' \
    --keys timestamp,username,ip,message \
    --metrics

docs.title: Cache Performance
docs.text:
Monitor cache hit rates:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.service == "cache"' \
    --exec 'if e.message.contains("hit") { track_count("cache_hits") }' \
    --exec 'if e.message.contains("miss") { track_count("cache_misses") }' \
    --exec 'track_count("cache_total")' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Service Dependencies
docs.text:
Track which services are interacting:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.has_path("downstream_service")' \
    --exec 'e.call = e.service + " -> " + e.downstream_service' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.call)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Hourly Health Report
docs.text:
Break down health by time:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.hour = e.timestamp.format("%Y-%m-%d %H:00")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.hour)' \
    --exec 'if e.level == "ERROR" { track_count(e.hour + "_errors") }' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Resource Exhaustion Detection
docs.text:
Find resource pressure points:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.level == "WARN" || e.level == "ERROR"' \
    --filter 'e.message.contains("memory") || e.message.contains("disk") || e.message.contains("connection")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --keys timestamp,service,level,message

docs.title: User Activity Tracking
docs.text:
Monitor user-facing operations:

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.has_path("user_id")' \
    --exec 'track_unique("active_users", e.user_id)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.get_path("operation", "unknown"))' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Last Hour's Health
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --since "1 hour ago" \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Compare Time Periods
docs.text:
# Morning traffic
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --since "2024-01-15 06:00:00" \
    --until "2024-01-15 12:00:00" \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --metrics

# Afternoon traffic
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --since "2024-01-15 12:00:00" \
    --until "2024-01-15 18:00:00" \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Real-Time Monitoring
docs.text:
Linux/macOSWindows 
> tail -f /var/log/app.log | kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --exec 'if e.level == "ERROR" { eprint("⚠️  ERROR in " + e.service) }' \
    --metrics

> Get-Content -Wait app.log | kelora -j \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --exec 'if e.level == "ERROR" { eprint("⚠️  ERROR in " + e.service) }' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Critical Error Detection
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.level == "CRITICAL"' \
    --exec 'eprint("🚨 CRITICAL: " + e.service + " - " + e.message)' \
    -qq

The -qq flag suppresses event output, showing only alerts.

docs.title: Threshold Alerts
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'if e.get_path("memory_percent", 0) > 90 { eprint("⚠️  High memory: " + e.service + " at " + e.memory_percent + "%") }' \
    --exec 'if e.get_path("duration_ms", 0) > 5000 { eprint("⚠️  Slow request: " + e.get_path("path", "unknown") + " took " + e.duration_ms + "ms") }' \
    -qq

docs.title: Service Down Detection
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.message.contains("unavailable") || e.message.contains("timeout") || e.message.contains("unreachable")' \
    --exec 'eprint("🔴 Service issue: " + e.service + " - " + e.message)' \
    --keys timestamp,service,message

docs.title: Prometheus-Style Metrics
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'track_count("http_requests_total")' \
    --exec 'if e.status >= 500 { track_count("http_requests_errors") }' \
    --exec 'track_avg("http_request_duration_ms", e.get_path("duration_ms", 0))' \
    --metrics

docs.title: JSON Export for Dashboards
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.level == "ERROR"' \
    --exec 'e.error_type = e.get_path("error.type", "unknown")' \
    --keys timestamp,service,error_type,message \
    -F json > errors.json

docs.title: CSV for Spreadsheets
docs.text:
> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'e.hour = e.timestamp.format("%Y-%m-%d %H:00")' \
    --keys hour,service,level,message \
    -F csv > health_report.csv

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
Large Log Files: 

> kelora -f json large-app.log.gz \
    --parallel \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service)' \
    --metrics

Sampling for Quick Analysis: 

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'if e.user_id.bucket() % 10 == 0 { track_count("sampled") }' \
    --metrics

Focus on Recent Events: 

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --since "30 minutes ago" \
    --exec 'track_count(e.level)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text:
Service health summary: 

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service + "_" + e.level)' \
    --metrics

Error rate calculation: 

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'track_count("total")' \
    --exec 'if e.level == "ERROR" { track_count("errors") }' \
    --metrics
# Calculate: errors / total * 100

Unique users: 

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --exec 'track_unique("users", e.user_id)' \
    --metrics

Service call patterns: 

> kelora -f json app.log \
    --filter 'e.has_path("operation")' \
    --exec 'track_count(e.service + "::" + e.operation)' \
    --metrics

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Missing fields: 

# Use safe access with defaults
e.get_path("nested.field", "default_value")

Inconsistent log formats: 

# Check if field exists before using
if e.has_path("duration_ms") {
    track_avg("duration", e.duration_ms)
}

Large numbers: 

# Convert to human-readable
e.duration_s = e.duration_ms / 1000
e.memory_mb = e.memory_bytes / 1024 / 1024
